name: Morris-Thorne-Yurtsever Wormhole Time Machine
description: A traversable wormhole whose mouths have been put out of step by taking one of them on a round trip at nearly the speed of light, described by Michael Morris, Kip Thorne, and Ulvi Yurtsever in 1988. Once the time shift between the mouths exceeds the light travel time between them, closed timelike curves loop through the throat, to the future of a Cauchy horizon whose light rays peel off one closed null geodesic.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

coordinates.name: External Lorentz
domains: |\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}_A(\tau)| \le b \;\text{in the rest frame of mouth } A = 1, 2 \;\text{(the balls removed)}
\mathcal{B}_1(\tau) \sim \mathcal{B}_2(\tau) \;\text{(the two spheres at equal proper time)}

parameters.description: Radius of each mouth: with $\mathbf{X}$ the position in space, $\mathbf{X}_A(\tau)$ the world line of mouth number $A$, 1 or 2, and $\mathcal{B}_1$ and $\mathcal{B}_2$ the spheres of radius $b$ about the two, the ball inside each sphere is removed

coordinates.convention: We use the Lorentz coordinates $(T, X, Y, Z)$ of the flat space outside the mouths, with $T$ carrying dimensions of time, and $\tau$ is the proper time along a mouth's world line. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Morris-Thorne-Yurtsever

parameters.description: Acceleration of the right mouth in its own asymptotic rest frame, where $g_{\max}$ is its greatest size, $g = \gamma^2\,dv/dt$ for a mouth moving at speed $v$ with $\gamma = (1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$
Form factor, dimensionless, which vanishes for $l \le 0$ and rises smoothly from 0 at the throat to 1 at the right mouth
Redshift function of the static wormhole, dimensionless and finite on the whole line
Areal radius of the static wormhole, a length, with its least value, the radius $r_0$, at the throat
Lapse of the accelerated frame, dimensionless, equal to 1 on the left half of the wormhole

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, l, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ the proper time of both mouths and $l$ the proper radial distance, negative on the left of the throat and positive on the right, and the polar axis $\theta = 0$ points along the acceleration. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Short Throat

parameters.description: Radius of each mouth, the least areal radius

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, l, \theta, \phi)$ in the rest frame of a mouth, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $l$ the proper radial distance, which rises from $-\infty$ to 0 toward one mouth and from 0 to $\infty$ away from the other, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

history: "What constraints do the laws of physics place on the activities of an arbitrarily advanced civilization?" asked Michael Morris, Kip Thorne, and Ulvi Yurtsever in 1988 [morris1988prl]. They handed their civilization a traversable wormhole, the short handle between two distant places that Morris and Thorne had designed for Carl Sagan's novel Contact, with its two mouths at rest near each other [morris1988prl, morris1988]. The left mouth stays where it is, while the right one is pulled, gravitationally or electrically, up to nearly the speed of light and then brought back [morris1988prl]. Seen from outside, the right mouth is the travelling twin and comes home having aged less than the left, while the time $t$ that runs through the wormhole is the proper time of both mouths [morris1988prl]. A traveller who enters the right mouth late enough leaves the left one at an earlier time, and can be back at the right mouth before setting out: a closed timelike curve [morris1988prl].¶Inside the wormhole and just outside its mouths they wrote the metric as $ds^2 = -(1 + glF\cos\theta)^2e^{2\Phi}dt^2 + dl^2 + r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$, in units with $G = c = 1$ [morris1988prl]. Here $\Phi(l)$ and $r(l)$ belong to the static wormhole, $g(t)$ is the acceleration of the right mouth, kept gentle enough that the wormhole holds its size and shape, and the form factor $F(l)$ rises from 0 at the throat to 1 at the right mouth [morris1988prl]. John Friedman and six coauthors, Thorne and Igor Novikov among them, made the throat arbitrarily short in 1990: they cut a ball of radius $b$ out of Minkowski space around each of two world lines and identified the two spheres at equal proper times [friedman1990]. That spacetime is flat everywhere except on the mouths, where the curvature is a delta function, and they called the round trip "twins-paradox motion" [friedman1990].¶A Cauchy horizon separates the region with closed timelike curves from the region without [morris1988prl]. On it lies one closed null geodesic, a light ray that leaves the left mouth, runs to the right mouth along the line joining them, passes through the throat, and arrives back at the event it left [morris1988prl, kim1991]. The rest of the horizon is made of light rays that peel off the closed one, which Sung-Won Kim and Thorne called a "fountain" [morris1988prl, kim1991]. In two dimensional Misner space, waves circling toward the horizon are boosted in frequency on every circuit, and their stress energy diverges there [morris1988prl, misner1967]. Morris, Thorne, and Yurtsever argued that the wormhole escapes this instability: its throat acts as a diverging lens, which cuts the amplitude of a wave by $r_0/2D$ on each round trip between mouths of radius $r_0$ a distance $D$ apart, and that can outweigh the boost [morris1988prl].¶A round trip is only one way to do it: Valery Frolov and Novikov showed in 1990 that a wormhole interacting with the matter and the gravitational field around it "almost inevitably" turns into a time machine [frolov1990]. Morris, Thorne, and Yurtsever had asked whether an advanced being could measure Schrödinger's cat to be alive, go back in time through the wormhole, and kill the cat before the measurement [morris1988prl]. Friedman and his coauthors proposed a principle of self consistency, "the only solutions to the laws of physics that can occur locally in the real Universe are those which are globally self-consistent", which Novikov had argued for in books of 1975 and 1983 [friedman1990]. For a class of static wormhole spacetimes with closed timelike curves, Friedman and Morris proved in 1991 that a massless scalar field with smooth data of finite energy at past null infinity has a smooth solution [friedman1991]. Fernando Echeverria, Gunnar Klinkhammer, and Thorne sent a billiard ball through the wormhole to strike its younger self, and found in 1991 that every such trajectory in a wide class has infinitely many self consistent solutions, which they summed up as "far too many solutions" [echeverria1991].¶Does the universe protect itself from time machines? Vacuum fluctuations of a quantum field loop through the wormhole, and their renormalized stress energy diverges at the Cauchy horizon: Kim and Thorne computed it in 1991 for a massless scalar field on a wormhole whose right mouth moves toward its left, and Frolov the same year for one whose time shift comes from a gravitational field [kim1991, frolov1991]. The divergence is weak: seen from a mouth at rest it disturbs the metric by $\delta g \sim (l_P/D)(l_P/\Delta t)$, with $l_P$ the Planck length and $\Delta t$ the proper time left before the horizon, which for mouths a meter apart is still $10^{-35}$ a Planck length from the horizon [kim1991]. Kim and Thorne conjectured that quantum gravity cuts the divergence off there and lets the closed timelike curves form [kim1991]. Stephen Hawking objected that $D$ and $\Delta t$ depend on the observer while their product does not, so that spacetime may stay classical until $D\Delta t \sim l_P^2$, where $\delta g$ reaches unity [kim1991, hawking1992]. He named his side of the argument the chronology protection conjecture: "The laws of physics do not allow the appearance of closed timelike curves" [hawking1992].¶Kim and Thorne wrote of the two conjectures that "It is not at all obvious to us now which conjecture (if either) is correct", and hoped that the attempt to test them "might produce insight into candidate theories of quantum gravity" [kim1991]. Casimir effects, disruption of the wormhole, and gravitational back reaction all oppose the time machine in the model wormholes Matt Visser studied in 1993, a "defense in depth" in which the back reaction grows large before the Planck scale is reached [visser1993]. On a Cauchy horizon whose light rays, followed into the past, all stay within a bounded region, a quantum field cannot be well behaved everywhere: Bernard Kay, Marek Radzikowski, and Robert Wald proved in 1997 that its renormalized stress energy is "necessarily ill-defined or singular" at the points where those rays accumulate [kay1997]. They read their theorems as support for Hawking's conjecture [kay1997].
